Accost

uh-KOST · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To accost is to approach and confront someone aggressively.

Two men accosted the cashier the moment she stepped outside for her break, demanding she hand over the store's key.

Worked Example

The paparazzi accosted the actress the second she stepped off the plane, crowding around her and shouting questions until security intervened.

Accost means to approach and confront someone aggressively -- the crowding and shouting make this an unwelcome, aggressive confrontation, not a friendly greeting.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

confront: To confront someone is to face them directly with a difficult matter -- and it can be calm, planned, even respectful. To accost someone is to come at them: a sudden, unwelcome, aggressive approach. You can confront a friend gently; you cannot accost anyone gently.

waylay: To waylay someone is to intercept them on their way -- lying in wait and stopping them before they reach where they are going. Accost shares the suddenness but centers the aggression of the approach itself; a fan can waylay a celebrity just to ask for an autograph.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

welcome: to greet someone warmly

greet: to address someone politely on meeting

Where it sits · how aggressive the encounter is — approach → accost → assault

approach vs. accost: Approach is far milder than accost -- to approach someone is only to come near them, the way a waiter approaches a table. To accost them is to come at them suddenly, aggressively, and unwelcome.

assault vs. accost: To assault someone is to physically attack them -- a far more violent and criminal act than accosting them.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ac-

prefix — ac-: a variant of ad-, meaning to or toward (Latin)

root — cost

root — cost: side, rib (as in the side of something) (Latin costa)

Put it together

Put it together: Accost comes from Latin ad- ('toward') + costa ('side, rib') -- literally 'to come up alongside' someone, which came to mean confronting them directly.

Use the root in a new word: coast

Use the root in a new word: coast: They drove along the coast for hours, watching the waves roll in.

Root Check

Word Choice

Accost carries a real sense of threat or unwanted aggression -- stronger than simply 'approaching' someone. It's distinct from antagonize (which provokes hostility without necessarily involving a face-to-face confrontation) and upbraid (a scolding for a specific fault, not a sudden confrontation).
